chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Wassa from Aban ibn Uthman from Abu Hamza al-Thumali who said:

I said to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) dealt with the people of the Qiblah (Muslims) in a manner contrary to the conduct of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) with the people of polytheism.' He said, 'He became angry, then sat down, then said: By Allah, he dealt with them with the conduct of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) on the Day of Conquest.'

Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) wrote to Malik, while he was at the forefront of his vanguard on the Day of Basra, instructing: 'Do not thrust (the spear) into one who is not facing you, do not kill a fleeing one, do not continue striking an injured one, and whoever closes his door, he is safe.'

So he took the letter and placed it in front of him upon the saddle before reading it, then said, 'Fight.' So they fought them until they made them enter the markets of Basra. Then he opened the letter, read it, then ordered a caller who called out with what was in the letter.

key_terms.سِيرَةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ: Conduct/Practice of the Messenger of Allah

ai.seo_question: What were the specific orders Imam Ali gave to Malik al-Ashtar during the Battle of Basra?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi highlights the strategic wisdom of Malik al-Ashtar during the Battle of Basra, illustrating the Shia scholarly view that his delay in reading Imam Ali’s (AS) letter was a calculated military decision to ensure victory before announcing terms of surrender, rather than an act of disobedience. The narrative reinforces the principle of 'Amn al-Dhimmah' (guarantee of safety) for those who close their doors, a key concept in Islamic jurisprudence regarding war booty and prisoners. It also connects to the broader theme of Imam Ali’s consistent adherence to the Prophet’s (PBUH) conduct, as affirmed by Imam al-Sajjad (AS) in the opening dialogue.
